messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Children Present: Being around children, Media / News: Related news, Known People: Related people
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mahmoud is a 78-year-old roofer who has worked on residential homes across the greater Detroit area for more than fifty years. He is a quiet, deliberate man, married for forty-eight years to his wife, Samira, with whom he raised three children and now has seven grandchildren. He came to therapy at the urging of his youngest son, who had grown worried about the changes he had seen in his father over the past year and a half. Mahmoud himself was not sure what talking could do, but he agreed because he had begun to feel that something inside him had come loose, and he no longer trusted himself to keep it contained.

The event that had changed everything occurred on a hot July afternoon in 2023. Mahmoud was working on a two-story colonial in Dearborn, replacing an old asphalt roof. The homeowner had mentioned that the attic had been used for decades to store old cans of paint, solvents, and pesticides, but Mahmoud had not thought much of it. He was on the roof, sweating through his shirt, when he noticed a strange sweet smell rising from the attic vents. Within minutes, his vision blurred, his throat tightened, and he felt a crushing pressure in his chest. He tried to call out to his crew, but his voice came out as a whisper. He remembers falling forward onto the shingles, his face pressed against the hot black surface, unable to move, certain that he was dying. He was later told that a combination of old chemicals had off-gassed in the attic heat, creating a toxic plume that had risen through the vents directly into his breathing zone. He spent four days in the hospital, and the doctors said he was lucky to be alive.

In the months that followed, Mahmoud found that he could not deliberately call up what happened on that roof. When he tried to remember the sequence of events, the details slipped away like water through his fingers. He knew the facts—the date, the address, the diagnosis—but the memory itself felt hollow, as though it belonged to someone else. What he could not control, however, was the way the experience would suddenly invade his present without warning. He would be sitting at the dinner table, and without any image or clear thought, his body would be flooded with the same terror, the same suffocating certainty that he was about to die. He would feel his throat close, his heart race, and he would have to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he would stand with his hands on the sink, waiting for the wave to pass. His wife would ask what was wrong, and he could not explain because there was nothing to point to—no picture in his mind, no memory, just the raw, wordless feeling of the event itself.

Mahmoud had always been a man who worked with his hands, who took pride in his physical strength and steadiness. Now he found himself unable to relax even in his own living room, which he knew was safe. He would sit in his recliner and find his shoulders locked, his jaw clenched, his eyes scanning the room for no reason he could name. At night, he lay awake for hours, his mind empty but his body alert, listening to the creak of the house, the hum of the refrigerator. When he finally did fall asleep, he woke frequently, often gasping, though he could never remember a dream. The most troubling symptom, and the one that finally pushed his son to insist on help, was his reaction to being touched. If Samira placed a hand on his shoulder from behind, he would flinch so violently that he once knocked a glass off the nightstand. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his own, that it was stuck in a state of permanent alarm, waiting for an attack that never came.

The triggers were not always obvious to him. He found that being around his own grandchildren, whom he had always adored, now made him irritable and restless. He could not bear the noise, the sudden movements, the way a child would run up and grab his leg without warning. He began to make excuses when his daughter invited the family over—he was tired, he had a headache, the drive was too long. He stopped watching the evening news because any story about chemical spills, factory accidents, or industrial disasters would send him into a spiral of dread that lasted for hours. He also avoided the men he had worked with for decades. One of them, a younger roofer named Tariq, had been on the roof with him that day and had called the ambulance. Mahmoud could not explain why, but seeing Tariq’s face made his stomach drop. He stopped answering his calls, stopped showing up at the coffee shop where the crew gathered on Saturday mornings. His relationships with his closest friends had quietly atrophied, and he knew they were hurt, but he could not bring himself to explain.

What finally brought Mahmoud to the clinic was a moment that frightened him more than anything else. He had been at the grocery store, standing in the cleaning aisle, when a woman’s child—maybe three years old—ran past him and accidentally bumped into his leg. Mahmoud had spun around, his arm raised, before he caught himself. The mother had stared at him, pulling her child close, and Mahmoud had walked out of the store without buying anything. He sat in his truck for twenty minutes, shaking. He had never in his life raised a hand to anyone, and the fact that his body had moved before his mind could stop it terrified him. He was afraid of what he might do next, afraid that the person he had always been was being replaced by someone he did not recognize. He came to therapy not because he believed it would help, but because he was now more afraid of staying the same than he was of talking about what had happened.
